27: Consider a circle of radius $1$ and the event that a random chord is longer than
28: the side of the inscribed equilateral triangle. Three natural models give three
29: different probabilities.
31: 1. If the chord is determined by a random central angle
32:    $\Theta\sim\mathrm{Unif}[0,\pi]$, then the event is $\{\Theta>2\pi/3\}$ and
33:    has probability $1/3$.
34: 2. If the chord is determined by choosing its midpoint uniformly on a fixed
35:    radius, then the event is that the midpoint lies within distance $1/2$ of the
36:    center, and has probability $1/2$.
37: 3. If the chord is determined by choosing its midpoint uniformly in the whole
38:    disk, then the same geometric condition gives probability $1/4$.
```

28: Assume AC. The triangular function $\tau(t)=(1-|t|)_+$ is the characteristic function of the probability density
29: $$f(x)=\frac{1-\cos x}{\pi x^2}\quad(x\ne0),\qquad f(0)=\frac1{2\pi}.$$
62: 1.1 First use $h(u)=(1-|u|)_+$ as a density in the space variable u. It is nonnegative Borel and $\int h=2\int_0^1(1-u)\,du=1$, so it defines a probability. Its characteristic function q has vanishing imaginary part by the oddness of $h(u)\sin(su)$. For $s\ne0$, integration by parts with $1-u$ and $\sin(su)/s$ yields $$q(s)=2\int_0^1(1-u)\cos(su)\,du=\frac2s\int_0^1\sin(su)\,du=\frac{2(1-\cos s)}{s^2}.$$ All factors and derivatives are continuous on $[0,1]$, so FTC and the bridge apply. Density integration is applied to the real and imaginary positive/negative parts. At s=0, q(0)=1, and continuity follows from the characteristic-function lemma. Thus q is nonnegative everywhere and bounded by one, with $q(s)\le4/s^2$ for $|s|\ge1$. The primitive $-1/s$ on $[1,R]$, the bridge and monotone convergence give $\int_1^\infty s^{-2}\,ds=1$; reflection gives the other tail. Hence q is integrable. [F1, F3, F4, F5, F7, F8, F9, F10, F11]
64: 2.1 Apply density inversion to that probability with characteristic function q. It supplies the continuous density $H(y)=(2\pi)^{-1}\int e^{-isy}q(s)\,ds$. This equals h everywhere: if the two continuous densities differed at y, continuity would give a small interval where their difference had one strict sign, contradicting that both densities integrate to the same interval mass. In particular $1=h(0)=H(0)=(2\pi)^{-1}\int q$. Therefore $f=q/(2\pi)$ is nonnegative and integrates to one, so defines a probability. It has exactly the displayed formula and the continuous value $1/(2\pi)$ at zero. [step 1.1, F2, F3]
66: 3.1 Density integration and the identity in step 2.1 now give $$\varphi_f(t)=\frac1{2\pi}\int e^{itx}q(x)\,dx=H(-t)=h(-t)=(1-|t|)_+.$$ This includes t=0 and both endpoints t=±1, where the value is zero; outside the closed interval it is zero as well. The density value at x=0 was fixed by continuity, not division by zero. AC is inherited from the compact bridge and density inversion. The argument applied inversion only to the known law h before establishing that the triangle is a characteristic function. [step 2.1, F1, F6, F9] ∎

26: Assume AC. Start with $r,g$ positive integers of red and green balls, and reinforce each drawn color by $c\ge1$. For integer $c$ this counts balls; the same construction works for real $c\ge1$ as color weights. If $R_n$ is the red count or weight after $n$ draws, then $R_n/(r+g+nc)$ is a bounded martingale for the draw-history filtration at every $n\ge0$.
46: 1.1 Use $\Omega=(0,1]$ with the trace Lebesgue sigma-algebra and length probability. Restriction is a measure by [F2] (equivalently restrict its event formula to subsets of $\Omega$), and [F1] gives total mass one. Define intervals for finite color words recursively: $I_{\varnothing}=(0,1]$. If $h$ has length $n$, contains $j$ red letters, and $I_h=(a,b]$, put $T_n=r+g+nc$ and $p_h=(r+cj)/T_n$. Then $0<p_h<1$ because both $r+cj$ and $g+c(n-j)$ are positive. Set $I_{hR}=(a,a+p_h(b-a)]$ and $I_{hG}=(a+p_h(b-a),b]$. Both are positive-length half-open intervals [[def-half-open-box]], disjoint with union $I_h$. Induction gives a finite partition at every depth, and each point has exactly one compatible word of every finite length. Thus every draw is defined on this one space by the interval containing the point; no infinite-product existence is assumed. [given, F1, F2]
48: 2.1 Let $\mathcal F_n$ consist of all unions of depth-n intervals. Complements and countable unions just select subsets of this finite partition, so it is a sigma-algebra. Refinement makes it a filtration. A word interval is exactly the intersection of the corresponding first n color events; conversely a color event up to n is a union of word intervals. Hence $\mathcal F_n$ is the draw-history sigma-algebra. On $I_h$ set $R_n=r+cj$ and $U_n=R_n/T_n$. These are finite-valued $\mathcal F_n$-measurable variables and $0<U_n<1$. If $J_{n+1}$ indicates the next red draw, then $\int_{I_h}J_{n+1}\,dP=P(I_{hR})=p_hP(I_h)=\int_{I_h}U_n\,dP$. Finite addition proves this identity for every event in $\mathcal F_n$. 50: 3.1 The pathwise update is $R_{n+1}=R_n+cJ_{n+1}$. The bounded $\mathcal F_n$-measurable $R_n$ is its own conditional version, since its event identities are tautologies. Since $T_n+c$ is deterministic and positive, conditional linearity gives $E[U_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n]=(R_n+cU_n)/(T_n+c)=R_n(1+c/T_n)/(T_n+c)=R_n/T_n=U_n$. Thus the bounded adapted process is a martingale [[def-martingale-submartingale-and-supermartingale]]. For $r=g=c=1$, $U_0=1/2$ and the first two possible new proportions are $2/3$ and $1/3$, each with probability $1/2$; their mean is $1/2$. After the first red draw the next proportions are $3/4$ and $1/2$ with probabilities $2/3$ and $1/3$, whose mean is $1/2+1/6=2/3$. 30: Let $R$ be a commutative unital ring, let $q,\rho\in R^\times$, put $z=q-q^{-1}$, and choose $\delta\in R$ with $z(\delta-1)=\rho-\rho^{-1}$. For $n\ge2$, the BMW algebra $BMW_n(R;q,\rho,\delta)$ is the unital associative $R$-algebra generated by invertible $g_i$ and elements $e_i$ for $1\le i<n$, subject to the following relations (an adjacent relation is imposed only when both indices exist):
32: - braid and distant braid: $g_i g_{i+1}g_i=g_{i+1}g_i g_{i+1}$ and $g_i g_j=g_jg_i$ for $|i-j|\ge2$;
36: - loop: $e_i^2=\delta e_i$.
40: If $z$ is invertible, the parameter relation reads $\delta=1+(\rho-\rho^{-1})/z$. If $z$ is not invertible, the presentation uses the universal coefficient relation $z(\delta-1)=\rho-\rho^{-1}$ and does not divide by $z$. The quotient by the two-sided ideal generated by all $e_i$ is the cup-cap-zero Hecke quotient; this definition does not assert a BMW diagram-basis theorem or a BMW quantum-centralizer theorem.
```

40: Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) for this norm-completion construction, and let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space. Order its finite-dimensional complex subspaces by inclusion. This is a directed system because the span $F+G$ of any two finite-dimensional subspaces is finite-dimensional. To each such $F$, assign the finite-dimensional CAR C*-algebra of [[thm-finite-dimensional-car-algebra-is-matrix-algebra]], with the generator-preserving maps of [[lem-car-finite-subspace-inclusions-are-isometric]]. Identify each stage with its image under these injective maps and let $\mathsf{CAR}_{\mathrm{loc}}(H)$ be their algebraic union.
42: The common finite-stage norm is well defined on this union because every inclusion is isometric. Under Countable Choice, [[thm-metric-completion-exists]] supplies a metric completion and [[thm-metric-completion-carries-a-unique-banach-space-structure]] equips it with the compatible Banach-space structure; this is the norm completion of [[def-completion-of-a-normed-space]]. Define the **CAR C*-algebra over $H$**, $\mathsf{CAR}(H)$, to be this norm completion of $\mathsf{CAR}_{\mathrm{loc}}(H)$. Addition, multiplication, scalar multiplication, and involution are the compatible finite-stage operations; submultiplicativity and isometry of the involution make them extend continuously to the completion, and the C*-identity passes to limits. The identity is nonzero because the zero-dimensional stage is $\mathbb C$ and every inclusion preserves its unit. For $f\in H$, write $c(f)$ for the image of the generator in the stage $\operatorname{span}\{f\}$; the universal inductive-limit property and its norm are proved in [[thm-general-car-has-universal-inductive-limit-norm]].
```

The remaining path starts at the exterior top point $i+2$: it follows the upper through strand to the first interface, the middle cap to position $i+1$, the upper cup to position $i$, the middle through strand to the second interface, the lower cap to position $i+1$, the middle cup to position $i+2$, and the lower through strand to exterior bottom point $i+2$. Thus the two remaining exterior endpoints are joined exactly as in $d_i$, and all six interface points lie on this path; no closed component is formed. The product is therefore $d_i d_{i+1}d_i=d_i$. Reflecting this three-position stack horizontally about its middle strand preserves stacking and loop counts while interchanging $d_i$ and $d_{i+1}$, so it gives $d_{i+1}d_i d_{i+1}=d_{i+1}$. If $i=m-1$, the site $m-1$ is either a defect or is paired to a site $k<m-1$ (it cannot be paired to a site inside $(m,n)$, since that would cross the arc $(m,n)$). If $i=m$, then $m+1$ lies inside the arc $(m,n)$ and must be paired to some $k$ with $m+1<k<n$. Stacking joins the distinct arcs $(m,n)$ and $(m+1,k)$, replacing them by $(m,m+1)$ and $(k,n)$; cutting at the arc ending at $n$ before or after this operation gives the same state, again with no loop removed. 33: $$1\le k_i\le j_i<n,\qquad j_i<j_{i+1},\qquad k_i<k_{i+1}$$
35: whenever the indicated indices occur, define the **Jones normal-form word**
37: $$N(j,k):=(u_{j_1}u_{j_1-1}\cdots u_{k_1})(u_{j_2}u_{j_2-1}\cdots u_{k_2})\cdots(u_{j_r}u_{j_r-1}\cdots u_{k_r});$$

Every generator monomial in $P_n(R,\delta)$ is equal either to $0$ or to $\delta^sN$ for some $s\ge0$ and $N\in\mathcal N_n$. The set $\mathcal N_n$ is in bijection with Dyck paths of semilength $n$; consequently it has $C_n$ elements and spans $P_n(R,\delta)$. This theorem asserts spanning and the count of the named candidates, not their linear independence.

For the empty word use east from $(0,0)$ to $(n,0)$ and then north to $(n,n)$. The inequalities $k_i\le j_i$, $j_i<j_{i+1}$ and $k_i<k_{i+1}$ say exactly that this path stays in $y\le x$. Conversely, in any path from $(0,0)$ to $(n,n)$ using east and north steps and staying in $y\le x$, record each positive vertical run whose $x$-coordinate is less than $n$ by its endpoint $(j_i,k_i)$; omit the forced final vertical run at $x=n$. There is no vertical run at $x=0$, every recorded run is preceded by a positive horizontal run, and consecutive recorded coordinates strictly increase in both coordinates. The path condition gives $k_i\le j_i$, while $j_i<n$ and $k_i<n$ by construction. Thus the corners recover exactly one admissible parameter list; if there are no recorded runs, it is the empty word. 34: V_{n+1,b}\!\downarrow_{K_n}\cong\bigoplus_{\substack{0\le a\le\ell-2\\|a-b|=1}}V_{n,a},
36: with each summand occurring once; vertices outside $\{0,\ldots,\ell-2\}$ contribute no summand.

([[def-temperley-lieb-type-a-path-spaces-and-matrix-unit-tower]])

50: 1.1 For any path $(a_0,\ldots,a_n,b)$ ending at $b$, its penultimate vertex $a$ is uniquely determined and satisfies $a\sim b$; deleting $b$ gives a unique prefix in $\mathsf P_{n,a}$. Conversely appending $b$ to any path in $\mathsf P_{n,a}$ with $a\sim b$ gives a path ending at $b$. Hence the set of paths ending at $b$ is the disjoint union of the appended path sets $\{pb:p\in\mathsf P_{n,a}\}$ over all such $a$. 56: 3.1 The identity of $K_n$ is $\sum_{a,p}E^{(n,a)}_{p,p}$. Its image is the sum of the diagonal units indexed by every one-step extension $pb$ of every length-$n$ path $p$; by step 1.1 each length-$(n+1)$ path occurs exactly once. This is the identity of $K_{n+1}$. For injectivity, every vertex $a$ has at least one neighbor in $A_{\ell-1}$, since $\ell\ge3$. For each source unit $E^{(n,a)}_{p,q}$ choose one neighbor $b$; the coordinate $E^{(n+1,b)}_{pb,qb}$ in its image determines the source unit uniquely by deleting the last vertex. Distinct source units therefore have disjoint image coordinates, so no nonzero linear combination maps to zero. Hence $\iota_n$ is a unital injective $*$-homomorphism and step 1.1 gives the multiplicity-one branching rule. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct] ∎

30: Let $B(0,r)\subseteq K\subseteq B(0,R)$ be a closed convex body in $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$. In any rotated coordinates set $C=\{y:\exists t,(y,t)\in K\}$ and $h(y)=\min\{t:(y,t)\in K\}$. Then $h$ is convex, finite on $B(0,r)$, and $L=2R/r$-Lipschitz on $B(0,r/2)$. Every interior point of $C$ has a subgradient, and every such subgradient at a point in the interior of this ball has norm at most $L$.
34: Finally, let $a\ge0$. If $x=-\|x\|e_n$ receives OUT and $h(y)\ge h(0)+\langle v,y\rangle-a\|y\|-b$ on $C$, then $s=(-v,1)/\|(-v,1)\|$ satisfies $\langle s,z\rangle\ge\langle s,x\rangle-aR-b-2R\varepsilon/r$ for every $z\in K$.
53: 1.1 Compactness of $K$ makes each nonempty vertical section compact, so its minimum exists; projection makes $C$ compact and convex. Convex combinations of two minimizing boundary points show convexity of $h$. For $\|y\|\le r$, the inner ball supplies a point at height zero, while the outer ball bounds all heights below by $-R$. Thus $-R\le h(y)\le0$ on that ball. [given, F1, F5, algebra]

55: 2.1 More generally on $B(0,d)$, $0<d<r$, let $y,y'$ be distinct and extend the directed line from $y$ through $y'$ by $r-d$ to $p=y'+(r-d)(y'-y)/\|y'-y\|$. Then $p\in B(0,r)$ and convexity on the segment $[y,p]$ gives $h(y')-h(y)\le R\|y'-y\|/(r-d)$. Exchange $y,y'$ and put $d=r/2$ to obtain the Lipschitz claim. [step 1.1, algebra]
56: 
57: 2.2 The ball $B((y,0),r/2)$ lies in $K$. Its convex hull with $(y,h(y))$ contains a ball of radius $\theta r/2$ about $(y,(1-\theta)h(y))$ for every $0\le\theta\le1$: combine the vertex with every point of that ball. Consequently all heights between $h(y)(1-2\varepsilon/r)$ and $-r/2$ lie in the inward $\varepsilon$-erosion, whenever this interval is nonempty. If $\varepsilon\ge r/2$ the claimed OUT bound is automatic from $h(y)\ge-R$ and $t\le-r/2$. For $0<\varepsilon<r/2$, write $H=-h(y)\le R$. If the interval is empty, then $H(1-2\varepsilon/r)<r/2$, so $H-r/2<2H\varepsilon/r\le2R\varepsilon/r$; every $t\le-r/2$ therefore satisfies $t<h(y)+2R\varepsilon/r$. If the interval is nonempty, OUT excludes its heights, so $t\le h(y)(1-2\varepsilon/r)\le h(y)+2R\varepsilon/r$. This uses an inclusion of balls, not an incorrect identity for the erosion of a cone. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

The truncated epigraph $E=\{(y,t):y\in C,\ h(y)\le t\le R+1\}$ is compact and convex: it is the image of the compact set of pairs consisting of a point of $K$ and a permitted upward vertical displacement. Fix interior $y$ and $p=(y,h(y))$. Let $p_j=p-e_n/j$, and let $q_j$ be its unique nearest point in $E$ by [F2]. Minimality along a segment gives $\langle q_j-p_j,w-q_j\rangle\ge0$ for all $w\in E$, by expanding squared distance and taking the right derivative at zero. Moreover $\|q_j-p\|\le2/j$. A subsequence of the unit normals $(q_j-p_j)/\|q_j-p_j\|$ converges by [F3] to a unit normal $(u,t)$ with $\langle(u,t),w-p\rangle\ge0$ on $E$. Upward vertical segments imply $t\ge0$; if $t=0$, interior displacements of $y$ in both horizontal directions force $u=0$, a contradiction. Thus $t>0$ and $-u/t$ is a subgradient of $h$ on $C$. At a point where the Lipschitz bound holds on a neighborhood, applying the subgradient inequality in the directions $\pm p/\|p\|$ gives $\|p\|\le L$. This proves the IN implication, also at the transverse-ball boundary by the bound from step 2.1 on slightly larger balls and passage to its limit. [F1, F5, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

33: For every $n\ge0$, the exact binary circuit of [[alg-qa-exact-binary-qft-circuit]] implements [[def-qa-cyclic-quantum-fourier-transform]] at $N=2^n$: it maps each computational basis vector $|x\rangle$, $0\le x<2^n$, to
35: $$2^{-n/2}\sum_{y=0}^{2^n-1}e^{2\pi ixy/2^n}|y\rangle,$$
37: with the declared output register order. Hence its denotation is $\operatorname{QFT}_{2^n}$ on every state. Reversing the gate list and replacing every gate by its adjoint gives the negative-sign inverse QFT with the same ideal gate count.
43: [F1] On a basis input $x=\sum_i x_i2^i$, the QFT output factors as $R_0\otimes\cdots\otimes R_{n-1}$ in the ordered output wires; before the final reversal it is $R_{n-1}\otimes\cdots\otimes R_0$ ([[lem-qa-binary-qft-product-factorization]]).
45: [F2] $H=2^{-1/2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathrm{CP}_s=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,1,e^{2\pi i/2^s})$ in control-first basis order; the ideal model also counts $\mathrm{CP}_s^\dagger=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,1,e^{-2\pi i/2^s})$ as one gate ([[def-qa-qft-gate-cost-model]]).
47: [F3] Ordered tensor factors retain the displayed wire order, and the final wire permutation reverses the corresponding product-basis factors ([[def-qc-tensor-register-and-permutation]]).
```

34: **Assume the axiom of choice** ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $M$ be a chosen $P$-graded type-one quantum weight module that is integrable, has finite-dimensional label-weight spaces and weight set contained in a finite union of cones $\lambda-Q_+$ ([[def-quantum-weight-module-and-integrability]]), and let $(L,B)$ be a crystal basis of $M$ ([[def-crystal-lattice-and-crystal-basis]]).
36: (i) **Splitting along the top isotypic part.** Let $\lambda$ be a maximal weight of $M$, put $N_0:=U_q(\mathfrak g)M_\lambda$ and let $N_1$ be the sum of the remaining simple constituents, so that $M=N_0\oplus N_1$ and $N_0\cong V(\lambda)^{\oplus m}$ with $m=\dim M_\lambda$. Then $L=(L\cap N_0)\oplus(L\cap N_1)$, $B=\bigl(B\cap(L\cap N_0)/q(L\cap N_0)\bigr)\sqcup\bigl(B\cap(L\cap N_1)/q(L\cap N_1)\bigr)$, and both pairs are crystal bases of $N_0$ and $N_1$.
38: (ii) **Uniqueness.** There is a locally weight-finite indexed family $(\lambda_j)_{j\in J}$ in $P^+$ and an isomorphism of $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-modules $\Phi:M\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\bigoplus_{j\in J}V(\lambda_j)$ with $\Phi(L)=\bigoplus_j\mathcal L(\lambda_j)$ and $\Phi$ inducing a bijection $B\to\bigsqcup_j\mathcal B(\lambda_j)$ of crystals. The multiset $\{\lambda_j:j\in J\}$ is the multiset of highest weights of the simple integrable constituents of $M$: the number of $j$ with $\lambda_j=\lambda$ equals the multiplicity $[M:V(\lambda)]$.
40: (iii) **Components.** Through $\Phi$ the connected components of the crystal $B$ are exactly the canonical highest weight crystals $\mathcal B(\lambda_j)$; each component has a unique highest weight element $b$, of dominant weight $\lambda$, and equals the lowering-generated subcrystal $F(b)$ of [[def-highest-weight-element-and-connected-highest-weight-crystal]]. In particular the crystal graph of any crystal basis of $M$ is determined up to isomorphism by $M$, and no other highest weight elements occur.
76: 6.1 Step G: locally finite iteration. Fix upper bounds $\lambda_a$ with $\mathrm{wt}(M)\subseteq\bigcup_{a=1}^s(\lambda_a-Q_+)$ and define $D(\nu):=\max\{\operatorname{ht}(\lambda_a-\nu):\lambda_a-\nu\in Q_+\}$. Each level $D(\nu)=n$ is finite, since it is contained in the finite union of root-height-$n$ slices of those cones. If $\tau>\nu$, every cone containing $\tau$ contains $\nu$, and $D(\tau)\le D(\nu)-\operatorname{ht}(\tau-\nu)<D(\nu)$. Thus, in increasing order of $D$, the highest weights of the simple constituents in [F1] are maximal among the remaining weights and may be peeled using steps 3.1-5.1. For a fixed weight $\mu$, only finitely many constituent tops $\nu\ge\mu$ occur: in each cone the nonnegative root coefficients of $\nu-\mu$ and $\lambda_a-\nu$ sum to those of $\lambda_a-\mu$. Each such top has finite multiplicity, bounded by $\dim M_\nu$. Consequently finitely many peelings exhaust every fixed weight space. The module decomposition of [F1] is algebraic, so every vector has finite constituent support; the compatible lattice and residue splittings therefore give $\Phi(L)=\bigoplus_{j\in J}\mathcal L(\lambda_j)$ and a crystal bijection $B\to\bigsqcup_j\mathcal B(\lambda_j)$ under an isomorphism $\Phi:M\to\bigoplus_jV(\lambda_j)$. The family is locally weight-finite and has exactly the constituent multiplicities of [F1]. AC permits the simultaneous top lifts used in these identifications. This proves (i) and (ii) without requiring $J$ finite. [step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, F1, F3, algebra]
78: 7.1 Step H: components. Under $\Phi$ the connected components of $B$ are exactly the $\mathcal B(\lambda_j)$: each $\mathcal B(\lambda_j)$ is connected because by [F4] every vertex is a lowering word from $b_{\lambda_j}$, and distinct copies share no vertices, so the partition into copies is the partition into connected components. Each $\mathcal B(\lambda_j)$ has highest weight element $b_{\lambda_j}$ of dominant weight $\lambda_j$ and equals $F(b_{\lambda_j})$ by [F5], and it has no other highest weight element by the uniqueness clause of [F5]; hence the highest weight elements of $B$ are exactly the $b_{\lambda_j}$, each generating its own component, and the crystal graph of $B$ is determined up to isomorphism by $M$. This proves (iii). [step 6.1, F4, F5, F7]

52: 2.1 The rank therefore drops at the apex. Moreover the cone contains the rays with directions $(1,0,1)$, $(1,0,-1)$, and $(0,1,1)$, which span $\mathbb R^3$; no single two-dimensional tangent plane at the apex contains all their velocities, so [L2] cannot supply a regular graph there. ```text
32: Inscribed triangulated surfaces with mesh tending to zero need not have areas tending to the surface-integral area of the cylinder; their areas can diverge to infinity.
36: **Given:** A cylinder of radius $r>0$ and height $H>0$; integers $n\ge2$ and $m\ge1$; and the Schwarz lantern with $m$ horizontal bands, $n$ vertices per ring, and successive rings staggered by angle $\pi/n$.
48: 1.1 Every vertex lies on the cylinder. Parametrize each triangular face affinely over the standard parameter triangle. Its constant parameter tangents are two edge vectors, so [L1] makes its area one half of their cross-product norm. Each of the $m$ bands contains $2n$ congruent triangles; expanding those edge-vector cross products gives total area $$A_{m,n}=2rn\sin(\pi/n)\sqrt{H^2+m^2r^2(1-\cos(\pi/n))^2}.$$ [given, L1, algebra]
50: 1.2 Take $m=n^3$. The maximum edge length is bounded by the sum of the vertical step $H/n^3$ and a circular chord of angle at most $2\pi/n$, so the mesh tends to zero by [L2]. [given, L2, algebra]
52: 2.1 By [L1], $n^2(1-\cos(\pi/n))=2(n\sin(\pi/(2n)))^2\to\pi^2/2$ using [L2]. Hence $n^3(1-\cos(\pi/n))$ grows like $(\pi^2/2)n$ and diverges by [L3]. [step 1.2, L1, L2, L3, algebra]
54: 3.1 Also $n\sin(\pi/n)\to\pi$ by [L2]. Substitution in step 1.1 and step 2.1 shows $A_{n^3,n}\to+\infty$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, L2, L3, algebra]
```

96: 2.1 Fix the trisection rule. Let $(u,v) \in I$ and $y \in \mathbb{R}$. Put $d = v - u > 0$, $s = u + d/3$ and $t = s + d/3$; then $u < s < t < v$ by step 1.2 and [L4], since $s - u = t - s = v - t = d/3 > 0$. The three pairs $(u,s)$, $(s,t)$, $(t,v)$ all lie in $I$ and their intervals are contained in $[u,v]$. Moreover $[u,s]$ and $[t,v]$ are disjoint, because $x \le s < t \le x$ is impossible; so $y$ fails to lie in at least one of the three. Define $T(u,v,y)$ to be the **first** of $(u,s)$, $(s,t)$, $(t,v)$, in that fixed order, whose interval does not contain $y$. This is a definition by cases on the three conditions $y \in [u,s]$, $y \in [s,t]$, $y \in [t,v]$, so $T : I \times \mathbb{R} \to I$ is a function and no choice is made. [step 1.2, L4, construct]
102: 5.1 Apply [L5] with $X = \mathbb{N} \times I$, $x_0 = (0, (p,q))$, which lies in $X$ because $p < q$ by step 3.1, and $F(n, (u,v)) = (\sigma(n), T(u, v, f(n)))$: this yields $h : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} \times I$ with $h(0) = x_0$ and $h(\sigma(n)) = F(h(n))$. An induction using [L6] shows the first coordinate of $h(n)$ is $n$, so we may write $h(n) = (n, (a_n, b_n))$ with $a_n < b_n$, $a_0 = p$, $b_0 = q$ and $(a_{\sigma(n)}, b_{\sigma(n)}) = T(a_n, b_n, f(n))$ for every $n$. By step 2.1 this gives $a_n \le a_{\sigma(n)}$, $b_{\sigma(n)} \le b_n$ and $f(n) \notin [a_{\sigma(n)}, b_{\sigma(n)}]$. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, L4, L5, L6, construct]
104: 6.1 For $m \le n$ one has $a_m \le a_n$ and $b_n \le b_m$, by induction on $n$ using step 5.1 and transitivity; consequently $a_m \le b_n$ for all $m, n$: if $m \le n$ then $a_m \le a_n < b_n$, and if $n \le m$ then $a_m < b_m \le b_n$, and any two naturals are comparable by [L6]. [step 5.1, L4, L6]
106: 7.1 The set $S = \{\, a_n : n \in \mathbb{N} \,\}$ is nonempty and bounded above by $b_0$ by step 6.1, so [L1] gives its least upper bound $x = \sup S$, unique by [L2]. [step 5.1, step 6.1, L1, L2]
108: 8.1 For every $n$: $a_n \le x$, because $x$ is an upper bound of $S$; and $x \le b_n$, because otherwise $\varepsilon := x - b_n > 0$ and [L3] would produce $a_m \in S$ with $b_n = x - \varepsilon < a_m$, contradicting $a_m \le b_n$ from step 6.1. Hence $x \in [a_n, b_n]$ for every $n$. [step 6.1, step 7.1, L1, L3, L4]
110: 9.1 Taking $n = 0$ in step 8.1 gives $x \in [a_0, b_0] = [p, q]$, and $[p,q] \subseteq (a,b)$ by step 3.1, so $x \in (a,b)$. Fix $n \in \mathbb{N}$: by step 8.1 applied to $\sigma(n)$, $x \in [a_{\sigma(n)}, b_{\sigma(n)}]$, whereas $f(n) \notin [a_{\sigma(n)}, b_{\sigma(n)}]$ by step 5.1, so $x \ne f(n) = g(n)$. As $n$ was arbitrary, the element $x$ of $(a,b)$ is not a value of $g$, contradicting the surjectivity of $g$ obtained in step 4.1. So no such pair $a < b$ exists: for every $a < b$ both $[a,b]$ and $(a,b)$ fail to be at most countable, that is, both are uncountable by [L7]. [step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, step 8.1, L7, discharge-contradiction] ∎

```text
33: An **elementary solid region** is a compact set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ supplied with a simple description in each of the three coordinate directions ([[def-simple-solid-region-in-a-coordinate-direction]]) together with one compatible finite patch presentation of $\partial E$ that is adapted to a simple description of $E$ in each of the three coordinate directions ([[def-adapted-outward-boundary-presentation-of-a-simple-solid-region]], [[def-finitely-patched-regular-surface-and-integrals]]).
35: Explicitly, the data are: three simple descriptions $(x,D_x,\gamma^x_1,\gamma^x_2)$, $(y,D_y,\gamma^y_1,\gamma^y_2)$ and $(z,D_z,\gamma^z_1,\gamma^z_2)$, each describing the same set $E$; one compatible finite patch presentation $\Sigma=\bigl((D_1,\varphi_1),\ldots,(D_P,\varphi_P)\bigr)$ whose patch images cover $\partial E$ and are contained in $\partial E$; and, for each of the three directions $k$, a partition of $\{1,\ldots,P\}$ into sublists $\Sigma^{+}_k,\Sigma^{-}_k,\Sigma^{0}_k$ making $\Sigma$ adapted to the $k$th description. The boundary is that of [[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]].
37: **One presentation, three partitions.** The patch list is the same in all three directions; only the sorting of its indices into upper, lower and lateral changes with $k$. That is what makes the three single-direction flux identities statements about one and the same boundary integral, and it is the whole content of the word "elementary" here.
43: - **A patch may be lateral in one direction and a face in another.** The six faces of a box illustrate both: the top and bottom faces are the upper and lower sublists for $k=z$ and lateral for $k=x$ and $k=y$. What cannot happen is a patch lateral in all three directions, and that is [[cor-every-face-of-an-elementary-solid-region-is-outward-oriented]].
```

Conversely $M^{(n)}_j \cap S_{n+1} = \varnothing$: a piece of $S_{n+1}$ coming from $i \ne j$ lies in $[e^{(n)}_i, e^{(n)}_i + \lambda_n]$, which is disjoint from $[e^{(n)}_j, e^{(n)}_j + \lambda_n] \supseteq M^{(n)}_j$ by step 1.3, while the two pieces coming from $j$ itself are disjoint from the open interval $M^{(n)}_j$ by [L10]. The common refinement may add collinear vertices to a vertical side, so each resulting two-dimensional cell is a convex polygon whose boundary carries all wall-subdivision vertices. These cells cover $P$, and two distinct cells meet only in a union of full consecutive wall segments, a common vertex, or not at all. [step 2.1, construct]

On a shared vertical wall, both adjacent cells use the same refined boundary segments, so triangles from opposite sides meet in a full common refined segment, a common endpoint, or not at all; within one cell the fan triangles meet in a full radial edge, the chosen interior point, or not at all. 39: Fix integers $M,q\ge1$, set $[M]=\{1,\ldots,M\}$, and write the image space on a fixed patch grid as $\mathcal X=(\mathbb R^q)^M$. A measurable space is a set with a specified sigma-algebra; equip $\mathcal X$ and a finite-dimensional latent space $\mathcal Z$ with such structures. An image is $x=(x_1,\ldots,x_M)\in\mathcal X$, with $q$ real pixel values in each of its $M$ patches. Let $S=(x^{(1)},\ldots,x^{(n)})$ be a finite training set with $n\ge1$. For $u\in\mathbb R^q$, set $\|u\|_2^2=\sum_{r=1}^q u_r^2$. For $V\subseteq[M]$ let $\mathcal Z^V=\{(z_j)_{j\in V}:z_j\in\mathcal Z\}$. For unmasked reconstruction, the encoder and decoder are deterministic measurable maps $E_\phi:\mathcal X\to\mathcal Z$ and $D_\psi:\mathcal Z\to\mathcal X$. For masked reconstruction, the encoder is a measurable deterministic map $(V,(x_j)_{j\in V})\mapsto(z_j)_{j\in V}\in\mathcal Z^V$, and the decoder maps the ordered length-$M$ sequence of encoded visible tokens and mask tokens to an element of $\mathcal X$. Each mask token is one learned vector $m\in\mathcal Z$ reused at every masked position. All maps take finite real values; when implemented by feedforward neural networks, each is a finite computation graph evaluated in the layered order of its vertices.
53: For masked autoencoding, fix an integer $k$ with $1\le k<M$ and let $\mathcal V_k=\{V\subseteq[M]:|V|=k\}$, a set with cardinality $\binom{M}{k}$. A mask $V$ is sampled uniformly from $\mathcal V_k$; the patches in $V$ are visible and the patches in $[M]\setminus V$ are masked. The encoder receives only the visible patches, with their positions, and no mask tokens. The decoder receives the encoded visible patches and a shared learned mask token at each missing position, with position information for all $M$ slots, and outputs predictions $\hat x_j(\phi,\psi;x,V)\in\mathbb R^q$ for every patch position.
60: For $T=T_{\rm norm}$, the masked-objective formulas below are defined only on $\mathcal D_{\rm norm}$, so a finite empirical objective requires $x^{(i)}\in\mathcal D_{\rm norm}$ for every $i$. For a population objective, require the event $A:=\{X\in\mathcal D_{\rm norm}\}$ to be measurable with $\mathbb P(A)=1$; interpret each loss integrand by its displayed formula on $A$ and by $0$ on $A^c$. Since $A^c$ is null, any other measurable extension there gives the same expectation. The raw target has no such restriction. The **per-example masked-patch mean squared error**, its population objective, and its finite empirical objective are
61: $$\ell_{\rm MAE}(\phi,\psi;x,V,T):=\frac1{(M-k)q}\sum_{j\in[M]\setminus V}\|\hat x_j(\phi,\psi;x,V)-T(x_j)\|_2^2,$$
62: $$R_{\rm MAE}(\phi,\psi;X,k,T):=\frac1{\binom Mk}\sum_{V\in\mathcal V_k}\mathbb E[\ell_{\rm MAE}(\phi,\psi;X,V,T)],$$
63: $$R_{\rm MAE}^{\rm emp}(\phi,\psi;S,k,T):=\frac1{n\binom Mk}\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{V\in\mathcal V_k}\ell_{\rm MAE}(\phi,\psi;x^{(i)},V,T).$$
64: The population objective averages the expectation over the image law for each fixed mask; equivalently, it is the joint expectation for an independent uniform mask. The finite empirical objective averages over every training image and mask.
```

59:    if $\dim(F_i\cap E_j)=\dim(F'_i\cap E'_j)$ for all $i,j$, if and only if

25: Let $f:X\to S$ and $g:Y\to S$ be morphisms of schemes. A **fibre product** is a scheme $P$, with projections $p:P\to X$ and $q:P\to Y$, such that $fp=gq$ and, for every scheme $T$ and morphisms $a:T\to X$, $b:T\to Y$ with $fa=gb$, there is exactly one $h:T\to P$ satisfying $ph=a$ and $qh=b$. Thus, naturally in every test scheme $T$,
26: $$\operatorname{Hom}(T,P)\cong\operatorname{Hom}(T,X)\times_{\operatorname{Hom}(T,S)}\operatorname{Hom}(T,Y).$$
27: Write $P=X\times_S Y$. The commutative square with edges $p,q,f,g$ is **Cartesian** when it has this universal property. Morphisms here are morphisms of locally ringed spaces, as in [[def-morphism-of-schemes]]. No existence assertion is part of the definition.
```

```text
29: In a finite DAG, a **route** is a finite sequence of vertices with consecutive vertices adjacent by an arrow in either direction; repeated vertices are allowed. Collider and noncollider status is assigned to each internal occurrence using its two incident route arrows. A route is **active given $C$** if each noncollider occurrence is outside $C$ and each collider occurrence is an ancestor of $C$, including membership in $C$. If an active route joins vertices $x,y\notin C$ with $x\ne y$, then an active distinct-vertex path joins $x$ and $y$ given $C$.
41: 1.1 Among active routes with these endpoints choose one of minimum length. If a repeated vertex occurs at an endpoint, discard the initial segment through the later occurrence of $x$, or the terminal segment from the earlier occurrence of $y$. Endpoints are outside $C$, and all retained internal occurrences have their old incidences, so the shortened route is active. Consequently any repetition in a minimum route consists of two internal occurrences of a vertex $v$. Delete the segment between two such occurrences and identify them. Only the two incidences at the joined occurrence of $v$ change. If $v\in C$, its old occurrences were both colliders, so the joined occurrence is still a collider. If $v\notin C$ and the joined occurrence is a noncollider, it is allowed; if it is a collider and $v$ is an ancestor of $C$, it is also allowed. [given, F1, choose, construct]
43: 2.1 The sole remaining possibility is that the join makes $v$ a collider although $v$ is not an ancestor of $C$. Both original occurrences were then noncolliders. The retained edge before the first occurrence points into $v$, so its deleted departure edge must point out of $v$; likewise the deleted arrival edge at the second occurrence points out of $v$, since its retained departure edge points into $v$. Traverse the deleted segment starting with its arrow out of $v$. There must be a first place where its arrows cease to point forward: the final arrow points backward, and an entirely forward return to $v$ would also contradict acyclicity. At that first change is a collider $w$, reached from $v$ by a directed segment. A directed segment in a DAG has no repetitions. Activity of the original route makes $w$ an ancestor of $C$, hence $v$ an ancestor of $C$, a contradiction. Thus every loop deletion above is active and strictly shorter, contradicting minimality. The minimum route is therefore a path. [F1, step 1.1, construct] ∎
```

34: For disjoint $X,Y,C\subseteq V$, $C$ d-separates $X$ and $Y$ in $G$ if and
36: undirected path from $X$ to $Y$.
42: [F1] A path is active exactly when it has no conditioned noncollider and
50: [F3] Every active finite route between distinct endpoints outside $C$ has an active path. [[lem-active-routes-in-a-finite-dag-have-active-paths]]
58: 1.1 Suppose an active path joins $X$ to $Y$. From any noncollider follow an outgoing path edge forward until reaching an endpoint or a collider. The reached endpoint is in $X\cup Y$, while a reached collider is an ancestor of $C$ by activity. Thus every path vertex is in $H=\operatorname{An}_G(X\cup Y\cup C)$. Replace each collider segment $u\to w\leftarrow v$ by its moral edge $u-v$; colliders cannot be consecutive along a path. The resulting walk avoids $C$, since all retained internal vertices were noncolliders and the endpoints are outside $C$. Loop deletion in this undirected graph yields a moral path avoiding $C$. [F1, F2, construct]
60: 1.2 Conversely suppose a moral path avoiding $C$ joins $X$ to $Y$. Keep its skeleton edges, and expand each remaining moral edge $u-v$ using a common child $w\in H$ as $u\to w\leftarrow v$. This is a finite route; its inserted occurrences are colliders and all its other occurrences are outside $C$. Every collider is in $H$. Call a collider occurrence bad if its vertex is not an ancestor of $C$. Among routes joining $X$ to $Y$ with every vertex in $H$ and every noncollider outside $C$, minimize the number of bad collider occurrences; the expanded route makes the class nonempty. If $w$ is a bad occurrence, it is an ancestor of some $s\in X\cup Y$. A directed path from $w$ to $s$ avoids $C$, since otherwise $w$ would be an ancestor of $C$. If $s\in X$, replace the whole prefix up to this occurrence of $w$ by that directed path traversed backward; if $s\in Y$, replace the suffix by the path traversed forward. If $w=s$, simply terminate at that occurrence. Otherwise the retained incident arrow points into $w$ and the new incident arrow points out of $w$, making it an allowed noncollider. All new internal chain occurrences are noncolliders outside $C$, and other retained occurrences have their original incidences. Intersections of the chain with the retained segment cause repetitions only; no loops are deleted in this step, and activity is defined occurrence by occurrence. At least the selected bad occurrence disappears and no new bad occurrence is introduced, contradicting minimality. Thus the minimum route is active. Its endpoints are distinct because $X,Y$ are disjoint, and [F3] gives an active path with those endpoints. [F1, F2, F3, construct, choose]

136: 1.3 **Crosscut claim.** Let $J$ be a Jordan curve with complementary regions $U$ (bounded) and $O$ (unbounded), let $p\ne q$ be points of $J$, and let $P$ be a simple polygonal arc from $p$ to $q$ whose remaining points all lie in one region $V$ of $\mathbb R^2\setminus J$; write $W$ for the region of $\mathbb R^2\setminus J$ different from $V$. Let $J_1,J_2$ be the two closed arcs of $J$ from $p$ to $q$ and put $D_i=J_i\cup P$. First, each $D_i$ is a Jordan curve: pasting parametrizations of $J_i$ and $P$ at their common endpoints gives a continuous bijection from the unit circle onto $D_i$, which is a homeomorphism because the unit circle is compact metric and $D_i$ carries the subspace topology and restricted metric of the plane; hence $D_i$ is compact and closed in the plane. [L7, L8] By [F1] if $J$ is a polygon, and otherwise by [A1, F2], each $D_i$ has exactly two complementary regions, and each of them has frontier $D_i$. Let $Z_i$ be the region of $\mathbb R^2\setminus D_i$ containing $W$, which is well defined because $W$ is connected and disjoint from $D_i$, and let $Y_i$ be the other region. Every point of $J\setminus J_i$ lies in $Z_i$: such a point $x$ has a ball $B$ about it disjoint from $D_i$, and $B$ meets $W$ because $x$ lies in the frontier of $W$, which is $J$; since $B$ is connected and contained in $\mathbb R^2\setminus D_i$, it lies in $Z_i$. Consequently $Y_i$ is disjoint from $J$, as it misses $J_i\subseteq D_i$ and misses $J\setminus J_i\subseteq Z_i$; being connected, $Y_i$ lies in one region of $\mathbb R^2\setminus J$, and since $W\subseteq Z_i$ it is not $W$, so $Y_i\subseteq V$. Next $Y_2\subseteq Z_1$: the set $Y_2$ misses $P\subseteq D_2$ and misses $J$, so it is contained in $\mathbb R^2\setminus D_1$; and $Y_2$ has points arbitrarily close to each point of the open arc $J_2\setminus\{p,q\}$, because the frontier of $Y_2$ is $D_2$; that arc is contained in $J\setminus J_1\subseteq Z_1$, and $Z_1$ is open, so $Y_2$ meets $Z_1$ and therefore lies in $Z_1$. Symmetrically $Y_1\subseteq Z_2$, so $Y_1\cap Y_2=\varnothing$. Now fix $x\in P\setminus\{p,q\}$. Because $P$ is a finite simple polygonal arc, choose a sufficiently small ball $B\subseteq V$ about $x$ that misses every nonlocal segment of $P$; then $B\cap P$ is just the one segment germ through $x$, or the two adjacent germs when $x$ is a polygonal vertex. Since $V$ misses $J$, we have $B\cap D_i=B\cap P$, so $B\setminus D_i=B\setminus P$ has exactly two connected local sides: two half-disks in the straight case and two sectors at a bend. Each local side is connected and contained in $\mathbb R^2\setminus D_i$, so it lies in $Z_i$ or in $Y_i$; as $x$ lies in the frontier of both $Z_i$ and $Y_i$, the ball $B$ meets both, so the two local sides receive opposite labels for each $i$; and no local side lies in both $Y_1$ and $Y_2$, because those sets are disjoint. Hence one local side lies in $Y_1$ and the other in $Y_2$. Finally let $N$ be a component of $V\setminus P$. It is open in the plane and closed in $V\setminus P$. Its closure in $V$ meets $P\setminus\{p,q\}$: otherwise it would be closed in $V$, and it is also open in $V$, so it would equal the connected set $V$, although the nonempty set $P\setminus\{p,q\}$ lies in $V$ and misses $V\setminus P$. So a ball $B\subseteq V$ about a point of that closure meets $N$, and $N$ misses $P$, so $N$ meets $B\setminus P$ and hence meets $Y_1\cup Y_2$. Since each $Y_i$ is open and has frontier $D_i$, which is disjoint from $V\setminus P$, each $Y_i$ is also closed in $V\setminus P$; the connected set $N$, meeting $Y_1\cup Y_2$, therefore lies in $Y_1$ or in $Y_2$. Hence $V\setminus P=Y_1\sqcup Y_2$ is exactly the decomposition into components, while $W$ remains a region of $\mathbb R^2\setminus(J\cup P)$ with frontier $J$. Therefore $\mathbb R^2\setminus(J\cup P)$ has exactly three regions, with frontiers $J,D_1,D_2$. The polygonal case of this claim is choice-free, and the arbitrary-Jordan case uses AC exactly through [F2]. [A1, F1, F2, L6, L7, L8]
138: 2.1 **Polygonal face induction.** Let now $G$ be $2$-connected and polygonally drawn. Build it by the ear decomposition of step 1.2 from any cycle, and induct on the number of added ears, with the invariant: every face of the current drawing has a simple cycle as its facial boundary walk, and the drawing satisfies $V-E+F=2$. For the initial cycle $C_0$, which is a polygon, [F1] gives exactly two regions with frontier $C_0$, so each facial boundary walk traverses the cycle once, and $V-E+F=|V|-|V|+2=2$. Assume the invariant for a drawing $H$, and let $Q$ be the next ear, a polygonal arc with distinct endpoints $u\ne v$ on the drawing of $H$ and with relative interior disjoint from that drawing. The relative interior of $Q$ is connected and lies in the complement of the drawing of $H$, so it is contained in a single face $F$; let $J$ be the boundary cycle of $F$ and let $V$ be the region of $\mathbb R^2\setminus J$ containing $F$. By [L4] the frontier of $F$ meets the drawing $X_H$ of $H$ exactly in $J$. Since a face is a component of the open complement of $X_H$, its frontier lies in $X_H$; hence $\operatorname{Fr}(F)=J$. If $F$ were a proper subset of $V$, [L6] would give a polygonal path in $V$ from a point of $F$ to a point of $V\setminus F$. The first point at which that path leaves the open set $F$ would lie in $\operatorname{Fr}(F)\cap V=J\cap V=\varnothing$. Thus $F=V$. Apply step 1.3 to the polygonal Jordan curve $J$, the distinct points $u,v\in J$ and the polygonal arc $Q$, whose relative interior lies in $V$: the two arcs $J_1,J_2$ of $J$ from $u$ to $v$ give graph cycles $D_i=J_i\cup Q$ of the new drawing, and $F\setminus Q=Y_1\sqcup Y_2$, where $Y_i$ is the region of $\mathbb R^2\setminus D_i$ that does not contain the region of $\mathbb R^2\setminus J$ different from $V$, and the frontier of $Y_i$ is $D_i$. Every other face $F'$ of $H$ is disjoint from $Q$, because the relative interior of $Q$ lies in $F$ and the endpoints of $Q$ lie in the drawing of $H$; so $F'$ is a connected subset of the complement of the new drawing, and it is closed there because its frontier lies in the drawing of $H$ and misses the relative interior of $Q$, which lies in the open face $F$. Distinct faces of $H$ remain distinct regions, and every point of the complement of the new drawing belongs either to an old face other than $F$ or to $F\setminus Q=Y_1\cup Y_2$. Hence the regions of the new drawing are exactly the faces of $H$ other than $F$, together with $Y_1$ and $Y_2$; their frontiers are the old boundary cycles together with $D_1$ and $D_2$, so the invariant passes to the new drawing. An ear with $k\ge1$ edges contributes $k-1$ new vertices, $k$ new edges and one new region, so $V-E+F$ is unchanged. Induction over the finitely many ears proves the facial-cycle and Euler claims for $G$. [F1, L4, L6, L7, step 1.2, step 1.3]
144: 4.1 **Hybrid induction.** Let now $G$ be $2$-connected, so $|V(G)|\ge3$ by [L2], and drawn as in the hybrid hypothesis: the cycle $C$ is drawn as a Jordan curve, and every other edge arc has its relative interior in the bounded region $U$ of $\mathbb R^2\setminus C$. Build $G$ by the ear decomposition of step 1.2 from the specified cycle $C$, and induct on the number of added ears, with the invariant: the exterior region of $C$ is a face with boundary cycle $C$, and every other face has a Jordan curve as frontier, that frontier being a graph cycle of the current drawing. For the initial drawing $C$, [F2] gives exactly two regions, the bounded $U$ and the exterior, each with frontier $C$, so both facial boundaries are the cycle $C$, and $V-E+F=|V|-|V|+2=2$. Let the next ear $Q$ with $k\ge1$ edges be added, with distinct endpoints $u\ne v$ on the drawing of $H$ and relative interior disjoint from it; by hypothesis that relative interior lies in $U$. It is connected, so it lies in a single face $F$ of $H$, and $F$ is not the exterior region, which is disjoint from $U$. Hence $F$ is a bounded face with a Jordan graph cycle $J$ as its frontier. Let $V$ be the region of $\mathbb R^2\setminus J$ containing $F$. If $F$ were a proper subset of $V$, [L6] would give a polygonal path in $V$ from a point of $F$ to a point of $V\setminus F$. The first point at which it leaves $F$ would lie in $\operatorname{Fr}(F)\cap V=J\cap V=\varnothing$. Thus $F=V$, and $V$ is the bounded region because $F\subseteq U$. In this AC-qualified hybrid argument, invoke [F2] for Jordan separation in the crosscut proof of step 1.3 even when $J$ happens to be polygonal; the optional [F1] choice-free branch of that earlier proof is not used here. Apply the bounded case of step 1.3 to $J$, $u,v$ and the polygonal arc $Q$: the curves $D_i=J_i\cup Q$ are Jordan curves and graph cycles of the new drawing, $F\setminus Q=Y_1\sqcup Y_2$, and the frontier of $Y_i$ is $D_i$. Every old face $F^{\prime}\ne F$ misses the relative interior of $Q$, so it remains connected and open in the complement of the new drawing. Its old frontier is a Jordan graph cycle contained in the old graph and hence in the new graph, so $F^{\prime}$ is also closed in that new complement. It therefore remains one component with the same frontier; the exterior region of $C$ is among these unchanged faces. Hence the invariant passes to the new drawing, and an ear with $k$ edges contributes $k-1$ vertices, $k$ edges and one region, so $V-E+F$ is unchanged. Induction over the finitely many ears proves both hybrid conclusions. All selections here are finite, and AC enters only through [F2], used for every Jordan crosscut in this hybrid argument. [A1, F2, L2, L6, L7, step 1.2, step 1.3] ∎

```text
38: [F1] A left action of a group $G$ on a space $E$ **by homeomorphisms** is a **covering-space action** when every $e\in E$ has an open neighbourhood $U$ such that $gU\cap U=\varnothing$ for every nonidentity $g\in G$ (def-group-action, def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps). Acting by homeomorphisms means that each map $e\mapsto g\cdot e$ is a homeomorphism of $E$; the underlying set action alone would not make the translates $gU$ open. This condition implies freeness (def-free-group-action) and makes the translates of $U$ pairwise disjoint. ([[def-covering-space-action]]).
40: [F2] A **covering map** is a continuous surjection $p:E\to B$ such that every $b\in B$ has an open neighbourhood $U$ for which $p^{-1}(U)$ is a disjoint union of open sets $V_j$, called **sheets**, and each restriction $p|_{V_j}:V_j\to U$ is a homeomorphism (def-continuous-map-top, def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps, def-disjoint-union-topology). Such a $U$ is **evenly covered**, and $p^{-1}(b)$ is the **fibre** over $b$. A covering is **trivial** when it is isomorphic over $B$ to a product projection $B\times F\to B$ with $F$ discrete. ([[def-covering-map-and-evenly-covered-neighbourhoods]]).
42: [F3] **The quotient topology.** Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space (def-topological-space), let $Y$ be a set and let $q : X \to Y$ be a surjection (def-injection-surjection-bijection). The **quotient topology** on $Y$ induced by $q$ is the final topology of the one-element family $(q)$ (def-initial-and-final-topology): $$\mathcal{T}_q \;:=\; \{\, V \subseteq Y : q^{-1}[V] \in \mathcal{T} \,\} .$$ That this is a topology is discharged in def-initial-and-final-topology, where every final topology is verified to satisfy (T1), (T2) and (T3). Dually, $C \subseteq Y$ is closed in $\mathcal{T}_q$ exactly when $q^{-1}[C]$ is closed in $X$, because $q^{-1}[Y \setminus V] = X \setminus q^{-1}[V]$. ([[def-quotient-topology]]).
44: [F4] For a covering $p:E\to B$, a **deck transformation** is an isomorphism $h:E\to E$ over $B$, so $p\circ h=p$ (def-map-and-isomorphism-of-covering-spaces). Deck transformations form the **deck group** $\operatorname{Deck}(p)$ under composition, and this group acts on $E$ by evaluation (def-group, def-group-action). ([[def-deck-transformation-and-deck-group]]).
54: 1.1 Let $U$ be a neighbourhood whose nonidentity translates are disjoint. Each $g$ acts by a homeomorphism of $E$ by [F1], so every translate $gU$ is open, and the full preimage of the orbit image of $U$ is $\bigcup_{g\in G}gU$, a disjoint union of open sets. That preimage being open makes the orbit image open in the quotient topology of [F3], and the orbit map is then an open continuous surjection, so [F6] applies to it. [given, F6, F3, F2, F1]
56: 2.1 Each translate maps homeomorphically onto that quotient neighbourhood. [step 1.1, F6, F2, F3]
60: 4.1 If the total space is path-connected, compare any deck transformation at one point with the unique group translate taking that point to its image; one-point determination then proves equality with that translate. [step 3.1, F4, F5, F1]
```

On bounded followup I read the full current lemma and full disk-data definition again. In step 1.9 e is explicitly the relative normal Euler number, 0=2mu+e is explicit, the construction seeks a framed disk, and the local definition says the specified framing extends exactly when its relative normal Euler obstruction vanishes. Thus make e0 means make e=0, and then the stated integer identity yields mu=0. All intersection labels are 1 in the explicitly simply connected inner-ball region, so this is consistent with the later group-ring mu=0 assertion; no e_0 or mu_0 is introduced. Step 1.8 says one surface disk and 2g bands, and its normal-product recipe supplies one meridian 1-handle from the disk and one index-2 handle per band, resolving the handle and CW cell dimensions/counts.
- Action: Typeset e=0 and mu=0, unmerge the precise handle/cell dimensions and counts and normal disk/plane dimensions, and restore numeric spacing and the unchanged coefficient list 1,-t,-t^{-1},1.
- Validation: current local checks passed; changed regions visually confirmed.
